parole.significato: A group of teleostean fishes having spiny fins. See Acanthopterygii.
parole.testo: Via taxonomic name Acanthopteri, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha, “thorn”) + πτερόν (pterón, “feather”).

parole.significato: Any member of the subclass Acari (aka Acarina): thus, a mite or a tick; specifically, any mite of the genus Acarus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Acarus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαρί (akarí, “cheese mite, tick”).

parole.significato: Any gastropod in the family Aglajidae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Aglajidae, from the type genus Aglaja. The genus name is borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀγλαΐα (Aglaḯa) and ἀγλαΐα (aglaḯa, “splendor, beauty”). Further from Ancient Greek ἀγλαός (aglaós, “splendid, shining”) and an earlier unattested *ἀγλαϝός (*aglawós).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Aglaonema of tropical foliage plants.
parole.testo: From the genus name taxonomic name Aglaonema, of Ancient Greek origin, from ἀγλαός (aglaós, “shining”) + νῆμα (nêma, “thread”).

parole.significato: Any of several plants, of the genus Alyssum, mostly of Eurasian origin, that have racemes of white or yellow flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Alyssum, from Ancient Greek ἄλυσσον (álusson).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the Ampelidaceae (now Vitaceae).
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Ampelidaceae (“former name of Vitaceae”) + -aceous, from Ancient Greek ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “grapevine”) + -ίδης (-ídēs, “-son, indicating a familial connection”) + -aceae (“-aceous, resembling”).

parole.significato: A vine of the genus Ampelopsis
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Ampelopsis, from Ancient Greek ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “vine”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “appearance”).

parole.significato: Any hookworm of the genus Ancylostoma.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the taxonomic name Ancylostoma, eventually from Ancient Greek ἀγκύλος (ankúlos, “curved”) and Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”). Analyzable as ancylo- + stoma.

parole.significato: Ankylosaurus magniventris, a large herbivorous dinosaur of the Cretaceous period notable for its heavy armor and clubli…
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Ankylosaurus, from ankylo- + -saurus, from Ancient Greek ἀγκύλος (ankúlos, “crooked”) + New Latin -saurus, from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”). The word was coined in 1908 without explanation by Barnum Brown and may refer to his mistaken belief that its back was sharply

parole.significato: A mosquito of the genus Anopheles, some insects of which transmit various parasites of the genus Plasmodium that are th…
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Anopheles (“genus of mosquitoes”), coined by the German entomologist Johann Wilhelm Meigen (1764–1845), from Ancient Greek ἀνωφελής (anōphelḗs, “unprofitable, useless; hurtful, prejudicial”), from ἀν- (an-) (a variant of ᾰ̓- (ă-, prefix forming terms having senses opposi

parole.significato: A reptile of the taxon Archosauria, which includes modern crocodilians and birds, as well as the extinct pterosaurs, no…
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Archosauria (“taxonomic division of extinct reptiles”), from Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn, “leader”) + σαύρα (saúra, “lizard”).

parole.significato: Any ungulate mammal with an even number of toes and belonging to the Artiodactyla, including pigs, sheep, deer, cattle,…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Artiodactyla, from Ancient Greek ἄρτιος (ártios, “even”) + δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger, toe”).

parole.significato: Any of various ornamental plants of the genus Baptisia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Baptisia, derived from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to immerse”), in reference to the plant's use as a source of dye.

parole.significato: Belonging to the clade †Ornithischia, a group of primarily herbivorous dinosaurs characterized by a pubis that projects…
parole.testo: Calque of taxonomic name Ornithischia, from Ancient Greek ὄρνις (órnis, “bird”) + ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”). In reference to the pelvic structures' superficial similarity to that of birds.

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Ctenanthe, family Marantaceae, native to Central and South America; commonly cultivate…
parole.testo: Borrowed from the taxonomic name Ctenanthe, from Ancient Greek κτεν- (kten-), the stem of Ancient Greek κτείς (kteís, “comb”) + New Latin -anthe, representing Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: A big-beaked prehistoric bird in the genus Gastornis, larger than the ostrich, believed to have become extinct 15- to 2…
parole.testo: From taxonomic name †Diatryma, a former name for the genus, from Ancient Greek διατρήμα (diatrḗma, “canoe”).

parole.significato: Any of the genus Gomphidius of mushrooms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Gomphidius, from Ancient Greek γομφος (gomphos, “plug”) + translingual -ius (“Latinizing suffix”).

parole.significato: Any of several shrubs, of the genus Hydrangea, having large clusters of white, pink or blue flowers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Hydrangea, from Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel, capsule”). Named by Carl Linnaeus after the shape of its fruits.

parole.significato: Belonging to the clade Saurischia, a group of dinosaurs typically characterised by a pelvic structure in which the pubi…
parole.testo: Calque of taxonomic name Saurischia, from Ancient Greek σαῦρος (saûros, “lizard”) + ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).

parole.significato: Any of various perennial, rushlike, herbaceous plants of the genus Lomandra, family Asparagaceae, largely native to Aus…
parole.testo: Borrowed from taxonomic name Lomandra, from Ancient Greek λῶμα (lôma, “border, fringe”) + Ancient Greek ἀνδρός (andrós, “husband”), referring to the circular border of the anthers.

parole.significato: A species of extinct shark that lived during the Miocene and Pliocene epochs (†Otodus megalodon).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name megalodon, from Ancient Greek μεγάλος (megálos, “big”) + ὀδών (odṓn, “tooth”). By surface analysis, megalo- + -odon.

parole.significato: Having a polyparium with a single row of cells.
parole.testo: From the now disused taxonomic name Monoprion (“section of genus Graptolithus”), coined by the French geologist and palaeontologist Joachim Barrande in 1850 from Ancient Greek μόνος (mónos, “single”) + πρίων (príōn, “a saw”), + -idian.

parole.significato: Any of several widely distributed evergreen flowering plants, of the genus Osmanthus.
parole.testo: From João de Loureiro's (1790) taxonomic name Osmanthus (“genus of flowering shrubs”), from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”), for the strong scent of the Osmanthus fragrans.

parole.significato: A large flightless bird of the order Rheiformes, native to South America.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from taxonomic name Rhea, from Ancient Greek Ῥέα (Rhéa, “the mother of Zeus in Greek mythology”).

parole.significato: A brontothere: any member of the family †Brontotheriidae of extinct odd-toed ungulates, some of which developed bony no…
parole.testo: A calque of taxonomic name Brontotheriidae, which is derived from Ancient Greek βροντή (brontḗ, “thunder”) + θηρίον (thēríon, “beast”) + -idae, or else from its probable source, calque of Lakota wakíŋyaŋ, conventionally translated as "thunder beast" when referring to these creatures, though also tra

parole.significato: Any of the order †Xenacanthiformes of extinct shark-like chondrichthyans.
parole.testo: From taxonomic name Xenacanthiformes, derived from the genus Xenacanthus [from Ancient Greek ξένος (xénos, “foreign, alien”) + ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “spine”)] + -iformes.
